## Report: hard-to-vary check on RFC 2001 (Stevens, January 1997)

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and abstract make one question central: *what should a TCP sender do about how fast it injects packets — and why — so it uses an internet of routers and slower links well without congesting it?* Range: any TCP connection over a path with a bottleneck or a router; standards track. Kind: a design question ("does it achieve its purpose"), resting on a causal core — that packet loss signals congestion. Held fixed through the tests below.

**2. The explanation, in parts (the author's words).**
A. `cwnd`, the congestion window: sender-side flow control; send `min(cwnd, advertised window)`.
B. Slow start: `cwnd` starts at one segment, +1 per ACK → exponential growth.
C. `ssthresh`: init 65535; on loss, set to half the current window, ≥2 segments.
D. The switch: `cwnd ≤ ssthresh` → slow start, else congestion avoidance.
E. Congestion avoidance: `cwnd += segsize²/cwnd` per ACK → ~one segment per RTT.
F. The assumption: damage-loss is <1%, so loss ≈ congestion.
G. Duplicate ACK on an out-of-order segment, undelayed.
H. Fast retransmit: three dup ACKs → resend, no timer wait.
I. Fast recovery: after H, congestion avoidance *not* slow start; `cwnd = ssthresh + 3·segsize`, +1 segsize per dup ACK, `cwnd = ssthresh` on the next new ACK.
J. The claim that adding `segsize/8` in CA is wrong.

**3. Part by part** (one mark each; never added up).

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| A `cwnd` | **Held** | Remove it: a new connection injects up to the advertised window (old TCP). The job "don't burst a router's queue" fails. |
| B slow start | **Held** | Remove it: cold start at full rate; throughput collapses ([2]). |
| B's *value* "1 segment" | **Loose** | Starting at 2 or 4 works as well. What is held is only "start small". |
| C concept of `ssthresh` | **Held** | Without it, nothing says where to stop ramping. |
| C's "half" | **Loose** | 1/4 or 3/4 would do; no reason for half is given. |
| C's "65535" | **Loose** | Just "larger than any window" at the time. |
| D switch rule | **Held** | One rule, two growth regimes. |
| E linear growth | **Held** | Remove it: exponential growth overshoots and keeps overshooting. |
| E's exact formula | **Two routes** | Any rule giving ~+1 segment per RTT does the job; the formula is one such. |
| F <1% assumption | **Held**, but its gauge is unstated | It is what lets loss stand for congestion. Which measurement holds it is never said. |
| G dup ACK | **Borrowed** | Rests on RFC 1122 (ref [1]); not tested here. |
| H's "3" | **Held if** | Held only by "one or two dup ACKs before a reordered segment". That depth is asserted, not measured. 3 vs 4 is free. |
| I fast recovery | **Held** | The argument — dup ACKs prove data still flowing — forbids slow start here. |
| I's inflation (3·segsize, +1/ACK) | **Built** | Worked out from segments that have left the network. |
| J `segsize/8` is wrong | **Unknown** | Asserted; no reason or reading given. It would take a case run at two growth rates. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Remove in groups:* removing B and E together (any growth) collapses A's job; removing C and D together leaves no switch. So the paper's support set is {A,B,C,D,E}, with I holding H.
*Swap:* half→quarter, 3→4, 1→2 all work. Each swap names the *held* thing as more general than the named one: "start small", "about half", "more than the usual reorder depth".
*Flip:* could the same parts explain that bursts never hurt? No. Could they equally say slow start is right after fast retransmit? No — the "still flowing" argument rules it out. Not a just-so story.
*Direction:* poke congestion → `cwnd` halves; poke `cwnd` (halve it) → loss eases. Both move, so it runs forward from cause, not backwards from result.
*Hidden in the starting points:* no. "Inject at the rate ACKs return" is stated openly as the explanation, not smuggled in as a label.
*Add a job:* "a connection that never loses still must not overshoot." Slow start + CA survives; the rival "reuse the last connection's window" fails on a changed path. The new job discriminates.
*Best rival:* open-loop pacing at a measured bandwidth. The telling change: capacity shifts mid-connection. Closed-loop loss feedback adapts; fixed pacing does not. Distinguishable, so the paper's account is testable and better here.
*Pull:* exponential ramp vs. careful growth pull at `ssthresh`; inflating `cwnd` in fast recovery vs. the risk of overflowing. The line is the asserted half.
*Catch-all:* "congestion somewhere" is bounded only by F, whose gauge is unstated. No gauge locates *which* router.
*Change list leaves out:* damage-loss >1% (a stated limit, but its gauge unset); receiver ACK delay beyond the advertised window; and the values 1, 3, 1/2, 65535, none derived.
*Provenance:* most parts are **borrowed** from Jacobson (refs [2],[3]) and the BSD implementation ([4],[5]) — the paper is documentation, so the working parts were fitted and built elsewhere. The values are **asserted/fixed** by current practice ("current implementations always perform slow start"). Only I's inflation terms are **built** in the text.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** (i) Give the halving fraction a gauge — run 1/2 against 1/4 on a path with a known bottleneck queue. (ii) Replace the asserted reorder depth with a measurement, so "3" is held by a reading, not habit. (iii) State and measure the <1% gauge. (iv) Mark "one segment" and "65535" openly as conventions.

**6. What this does not show.** Passing is not truth. These are fitted, widely-deployed algorithms; the check shows which parts are pinned and which are conventions, not that the design is optimal. It is not a check on how accurate any forecast was.

**7. One next step.** Pick the halving fraction. Before running anything, write down what 1/2 and 1/4 each predict when the bottleneck queue size changes; then run it.

Range: any TCP connection over an internet with a bottleneck or router; standards track. Kind: mostly "does it achieve its purpose" (design), resting on a causal core — loss signals congestion.

A. cwnd, congestion window, sender-side flow control; send min(cwnd, advertised window).
B. slow start: cwnd=1 segment, +1 per ACK → exponential.
C. ssthresh, init 65535; on loss set to half the current window, ≥2 segments.
D. switch rule: cwnd ≤ ssthresh → slow start, else congestion avoidance.
E. congestion avoidance: cwnd += segsize²/cwnd per ACK → ~1 segment per RTT.
F. loss-by-damage <1% assumption, so loss ≈ congestion.
G. duplicate ACK on out-of-order segment, undelayed.
H. fast retransmit: 3 dup ACKs → retransmit, no timer wait.

- A cwnd — held (J1: removes the burst that overruns router queues).

- B's "one segment" initial value — loose (2 or 4 would do; only "start small" is held).
- C ssthresh as a concept — held (job: where to stop ramping and turn careful).

- E linear growth, "one segment per RTT" — held (job: avoid overshoot after halving); the exact formula segsize²/cwnd is a mechanical consequence, two routes (any rule giving +1 seg/RTT).
- F <1% assumption — held (it is the gauge that lets loss stand for congestion) but borrowed/declared; the gauge is unstated.
- G dup ACK — borrowed (RFC 1122) — held by H's job.
- H 3-dup-ACK threshold — held if (held only by "usual reorder depth is 1–2", which is asserted, not measured); 3 vs 4 free.
- I fast recovery — held (job: don't cut flow when dup ACKs show data still flowing); the inflation terms +3, +1 — held by a mechanism (segments that left the network) — built.
